newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Cosmo plans to buy Iraq oil after UN deal.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Cosmo plans to buy Iraq oil after UN deal.

text.p: Refiner Cosmo Oil Co Ltd said on Thursday it planned to buy Iraqi crude under a term contract after the oil-for-food deal between the United Nations and Iraq is implemented.
"We plan to buy Iraqi crude under a term contract when exports resume," a Cosmo Oil official told Reuters in an interview.

"The quality of Iraqi crude is of no problem and we are looking forward to Iraq's return to the market," Nobuyuki Kitamura, Deputy General Manager of Cosmo Oil's International Petroleum Department said.
He said the problem of shipments would need to be cleared before imports would be possible.
Japanese tankers will not sail to the Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr, where Iraq exports to Asia are due to leave, until the safety of port facilities and surrounding areas are confirmed.

Under the oil-for-food scheme, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months in order to buy food and supplies for civilians suffering from sanctions imposed by the U.N. after Baghdad invaded Kuwait in 1990. At current prices exports are expected to be about 550,000 barrels-per-day (bpd).
Iraqi oil flows await final approval by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in the form of a "final report" to be submitted to the security council.
Diplomats and U.N. officials expect the report in December, possibly around December 10-15.

Cosmo Oil used to import 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi crude before the sanctions were imposed, which accounts for about five percent of the company's total imports of 552,554 bpd in calendar 1995.
Oil industry sources view Cosmo Oil and Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd, which both process large quantities of medium grade, sour crudes, as leading candidates as the first Japanese importers of Iraqi crude.
Kitamura said Cosmo planned to shave spot crude purchases when it started importing Iraqi crude.
"We would cut down on spot purchases, which account for about 20 percent of our total crude imports," Kitamura said.

One expected change in the buying pattern of Iraqi crude, compared to six years back, would be that most Japanese oil firms are likely to try conclude deals with Iraq, without going through trading houses, Kitamura said.
"More and more Japanese oil firms now negotiate directly with oil producers," he said.
Oil industry sources said previous Iraqi crude imports were almost totally handled by Mitsubishi Corp
Increasing dependency on the Middle East for crude supplies was of no worry for Cosmo Oil, Kitamura said.
After experiencing two oil shocks in the 1970s, Japanese oil firms have tried their best to diversify suppliers away from the Middle East.
However, in recent years, the Middle East had proven itself to be a reliable and stable producer, Kitamura said.
"Our company's dependency on the Middle East may rise slightly more," Kitamura said. "We want to have close ties with Middle Eastern coutries," he said.
Cosmo Oil's dependency on the Middle East has risen from 84.6 percent in calendar 1994 to 88.3 percent in October 1996.
Japan's oil industry's average dependency on the Middle East was about 75 percent in 1995.
Iraq, the second biggest oil producer in OPEC after Saudi Arabia before the Gulf War, produced 3.5 million bpd of crude in July 1990, a month before it invaded Kuwait.
Japan was a major buyer of Iraqi crude with imports reaching about 190,000 bpd.
